courseEvidence.name: Personal & Professional Development
courseEvidence.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
courseEvidence.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
courseEvidence.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design
courseEvidence.contribution: Develops academic writing, research literacy and civic reflection.

courseEvidence.name: Microeconomics & Behavior
courseEvidence.description2: Study how consumers and producers make decisions under scarcity. Explore key concepts such as rational choice, decision-making under uncertainty, and non-egoistic preferences. Analyze market structures, strategic interactions, and factor markets. Learn how markets function and examine the impact of regulation. Develop analytical tools to better understand behavior and engage with empirical research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops microeconomic theory through consumer behaviour, imperfectly competitive markets and economy-wide allocation. Students examine choice under uncertainty, non-egoistic preferences and cognitive limitations, then monopoly, strategic behaviour and labour and capital markets. General equilibrium, efficiency, externalities and government complete the analysis. Algebraic problem-solving and graphical analysis are connected to the interpretation and evaluation of research papers.
courseEvidence.topics: Choice under uncertainty; Non-egoistic preferences; Cognitive limitations; Monopoly; Imperfect competition and strategic behaviour; Labour markets; Capital markets; General equilibrium; Market efficiency; Externalities; Government intervention
courseEvidence.methods: Algebraic microeconomic analysis; Graphical economic analysis; Critical evaluation of economic research
courseEvidence.contribution: adds microeconomic and behavioural analysis of individual and institutional decision-making

courseEvidence.name: Econometrics
courseEvidence.description2: Econometrics supplies tools to analyze data to answer questions of causality and prediction. In this course you learn three estimators—Ordinary Least Squares, Generalized Least Squares, and Instrumental Variables—and three tests—t-test, F-test, and LM-test. Understanding the basic rules of econometrics, particularly the sampling distribution concept, is key, and the course uses Monte Carlo simulations in Stata to visualize it. Tools are applied to estimate economic relationships and make predictions, and students write an empirical paper.
courseEvidence.contribution: Estimates economic relationships, tests hypotheses and evaluates causal and predictive claims using regression and instrumental variables.

courseEvidence.name: Behavioral Economics
courseEvidence.description2: This course integrates insights from psychology into economic theory to better understand how people make decisions. Learn how actual behavior deviates from the predictions of traditional economic models due to biases, heuristics, and framing. Through experiments, students will deepen their understanding of decision-making and its implications for economic theory and practice.
courseEvidence.contribution: connects psychological evidence to economic decision-making, biases and behavioural choice

courseEvidence.name: Marketing & Consumer Engagement
courseEvidence.description2: This course unpacks what drives consumer engagement with brands and how marketers build customer trust responsibly. It introduces key marketing concepts, consumer psychology, AI/technology-driven marketing innovation, and brand and communication strategies. Students will explore real-life case studies, develop a strategic marketing plan and learn how marketers build sustainable brand strategies.
courseEvidence.profile: Connects marketing strategy and consumer psychology to responsible brand development and customer engagement. Students study strategic planning, customer experience, qualitative and quantitative insights, brand identity, digital marketing and behavioural framing. Applied projects analyze a company's strategy and response to disruption, design a brand, and investigate a consumer phenomenon using academic literature and primary and secondary evidence. Customer-journey mapping translates findings into recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Strategic marketing planning; Marketing mix; Customer centricity and experience; Consumer journeys; Market research and augmented insights; Brand identity and image; Brand partnerships; Digital and social marketing; Responsible marketing; Consumer psychology; Nudging and framing; Emerging technologies and marketing agility
courseEvidence.methods: Marketing-strategy case analysis; Advertising-campaign analysis; Kapferer brand-identity prism; Brand design; Primary and secondary consumer research; Consumer-journey mapping; Disruption-response planning
courseEvidence.contribution: Examines consumer engagement and market communication, applying behavioural ideas to marketing decisions.

courseEvidence.name: Market Research
courseEvidence.description2: See how companies figure out what customers love and what they don’t. You’ll plan and carry out real research, analyze what you find, and share your results. Our course shows you how to gather opinions and turn them into smart business ideas. Ready to turn curiosity into career skills? Perfect for future marketers, analysts, or entrepreneurs.
courseEvidence.contribution: provides applied research design, data gathering and analysis in organisational and market contexts

courseEvidence.name: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations
courseEvidence.description2: Through experiential learning, students turn their own bold ideas into new ventures. No prior business expertise is required as teams work on a startup project from ideation to final pitch while gaining business and entrepreneurial skills in areas such as design thinking, business model and customer validation. The class fosters creativity and collaboration to drive business and social innovation.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces entrepreneurship and core business functions through the development of a startup concept. Students use design thinking to discover customer needs, define a problem, generate and prototype solutions, and construct value propositions and business models. Marketing, finance, operations, human resources and funding inform a coherent business plan and investor pitch. Entrepreneurial cases and a startup simulation examine decision-making, early growth and business lifecycles, with attention to societal impact and sustainability.
courseEvidence.topics: Entrepreneurial mindset and pathways; Business environments, ownership and competition; Customer needs; Value propositions; Business models; Marketing and sales; Finance and accounting; Venture funding; Operations and human resources; Competitive positioning; Startup growth and business lifecycles; Sustainability and societal impact
courseEvidence.methods: Design thinking; Customer-needs discovery; Ideation and prototyping; Value Proposition Canvas; Business Model Canvas; Business planning; SWOT and risk assessment; Startup simulation
courseEvidence.contribution: provides foundational understanding of organisations, entrepreneurship and business decision-making

courseEvidence.name: Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: Research Methods & Statistics gives you a strong foundation in how business management—and social and behavioral sciences—move from mere practices to true fields of scientific study. You’ll learn how to plan research logically, from designing studies to working with real data using experimental and survey techniques. You’ll also study descriptive and inferential statistics, with a brief intro to multivariate tools.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces empirical research design and statistical analysis, followed by a substantial student research project. Students study operationalization, measurement quality, sampling, surveys and experimental and nonexperimental designs, then descriptive statistics, estimation, hypothesis testing and introductory regression. R and R Commander support data display and analysis. Project teams develop instruments and a research plan, collect and analyze data, and report results under explicit research-ethics and privacy requirements.
courseEvidence.topics: Scientific inquiry and hypotheses; Operationalization and measurement; Reliability and validity; Survey construction and sampling; Randomized and quasi-experimental designs; Nonexperimental and qualitative research; Descriptive statistics; Sampling distributions and estimation; Hypothesis testing and confidence intervals; Association and regression; Research ethics and anonymous data collection
courseEvidence.methods: Survey design; Probability and nonprobability sampling; Experimental and nonexperimental research design; R and R Commander data analysis; Descriptive statistics and visualization; Scale-reliability analysis; One- and two-sample mean tests; ANOVA; Chi-square tests; Correlation and regression; Empirical data collection and analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides foundational empirical research design and statistical analysis

courseEvidence.name: Personal Leadership
courseEvidence.description2: Personal Leadership provides a comprehensive introduction to leadership theory and practice, designed to help students discover their unique leadership style through self-awareness and practical skill-building. Through interactive workshops, reflective exercises, and real-world applications, students engage deeply with core leadership principles and develop the tools needed to lead confidently in any setting.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces leadership through self-leadership, leadership theory and emotional intelligence. Covey's habits provide a framework for personal vision, prioritization and collaboration, alongside transformational, authentic, situational and adaptive leadership perspectives. Students analyze personality and emotional-intelligence profiles in relation to group dynamics, examine leadership cases, and construct a personal development plan with actionable goals. Assessment tools support educational reflection rather than diagnosis, and the outline acknowledges differences in their scientific support.
courseEvidence.topics: Self-leadership and self-awareness; Covey's seven habits; Emotional intelligence and emotion regulation; Personality and group dynamics; Transformational and authentic leadership; Situational and adaptive leadership; Evolutionary perspectives on leadership; Goal setting and prioritization; Conflict resolution and negotiation; Trust and collaboration
courseEvidence.methods: Leadership theory and case analysis; Reflective personality and emotional-intelligence assessments; Eisenhower prioritization matrix; SMART goal setting; Leadership-development planning; Leadership simulations
courseEvidence.contribution: provides foundational leadership theory, self-awareness and applied leadership skills

courseEvidence.name: Leadership Communication
courseEvidence.description2: This course blends theory with practice from both fiction and the real world, helping you develop essential leadership skills. Learn how to inspire teams, sharpen your communication, take ethical decisions, and lead with confidence.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies leadership communication through leadership theory, persuasion and practical rhetorical work. Students compare contemporary leadership approaches and examine emotional intelligence, gender, culture and ethics. Literary characters, film and speeches provide material for analyzing effective and ineffective leadership. Students interview a real leader, analyze the leader's communication challenge in an advisory report, and develop a public address presenting their own ethical leadership vision.
courseEvidence.topics: Leadership models and approaches; Transformational, authentic and adaptive leadership; Servant leadership and followership; Emotional intelligence; Leadership ethics; Gender and culture in leadership; Persuasion and organizational communication; Leadership in literature and film; Storytelling and public speaking; Personal leadership vision
courseEvidence.methods: Leadership-theory application; Literary and film-based leadership analysis; Professional interviewing and note collection; Leadership-discourse analysis; Communication-advisory report development; Rhetorical speechwriting and storytelling
courseEvidence.contribution: develops leadership communication, ethics and interpersonal influence

courseEvidence.name: Psychology of Leading Under Pressure
courseEvidence.description2: What does it take to lead effectively through pressure, conflict, and diversity? Explore how emotion, identity, belonging, and inclusion shape leadership, teamwork, and performance. Design and conduct an original empirical study while building career-ready skills in research design, data analysis, teamwork, ethical decision-making, and scientific communication.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how emotion regulation, emotional intelligence, emotional expression and suppression, emotional labor, belonging, identity safety and psychological safety shape leadership and social interaction under conflict, exclusion and interpersonal uncertainty. It emphasises inclusive leadership and ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences, with digital emotion regulation as a further strand. Students conduct a supervised quantitative survey project: formulating theory-driven hypotheses, selecting established psychological measures, designing and piloting a Qualtrics survey, recruiting participants ethically, collecting original data and preparing a clean dataset. Individual work applies descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, correlations, group comparisons and introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio, and interprets findings and limitations in empirical reports and evidence-based leadership recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Emotion regulation strategies; Emotional intelligence; Emotional expression and suppression; Emotional labor; Inclusive leadership; Belonging and identity safety; Psychological safety; Ethnic, cultural, sexual and gender minority experiences; Digital emotion regulation; Psychological measurement, reliability and validity; Ethical survey research in diverse populations; Interpretation and limitations of quantitative evidence; Evidence-based leadership recommendations
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-driven hypothesis formulation; Quantitative survey research; Established psychological measure selection and evaluation; Qualtrics survey construction and piloting; Ethical participant recruitment and original data collection; Codebook development, reverse coding and scale scoring; Data cleaning and missing-data documentation; Descriptive statistics; Reliability analysis; Correlation analysis; Group comparisons; Introductory multiple regression in SPSS or RStudio; APA-style empirical reporting
courseEvidence.contribution: Examines emotion regulation, identity and belonging in leadership under pressure.

courseEvidence.name: Psychology of Organizations & Leadership
courseEvidence.description2: This course offers Liberal Arts and Sciences students a deep dive into the psychological, social, and structural dynamics that shape workplaces. Through interactive case discussions, simulations, and real-world insights, students develop critical skills in motivation, leadership, group dynamics, and culture. By synthesizing research and applying theory to practice, participants gain the tools to navigate and influence diverse organizational environments effectively.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines organizational behaviour at individual, group and organizational levels. Topics connect personality, perception, emotions and motivation to teams, leadership, power, conflict, structure, culture and change. Students design research plans for organizational cases and conduct a brief systematic literature review using PRISMA reporting tools. Workshops develop literature searching, study selection, source appraisal and synthesis, linking organizational-psychology evidence to practical questions and recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Diversity, equity and inclusion; Job attitudes and satisfaction; Emotions, stress and workplace health; Personality and individual differences; Perception and decision-making; Motivation; Group behaviour and work teams; Human resource systems; Communication, conflict and negotiation; Leadership, power and politics; Organizational structure; Organizational culture and change
courseEvidence.methods: Organizational case analysis; Research design and hypothesis formulation; Systematic literature review; PRISMA flow diagrams and checklists; Database searching and study screening; Source-quality appraisal and evidence synthesis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides organisational-psychology theory on motivation, leadership, groups and organisational culture

courseEvidence.name: Negotiation & Strategic Thinking
courseEvidence.description2: How do you get to yes? In this course you will learn how to craft persuasive arguments, deploy the right language, negotiate more effectively, and influence decisions with confidence—whether in business, leadership, or life.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops negotiation as an analytical practice and interpersonal skill. Students learn interest-based bargaining, BATNA and ZOPA, value creation, framing, concessions and strategies for handling power, emotions and difficult counterparts. Social-psychological and communication perspectives connect negotiation to trust, ethics, culture and relationships. Frequent simulations and narrative analysis lead to an annotated negotiation film and the design, teaching and evaluation of a negotiation scenario grounded in Delta Climate Center themes.
courseEvidence.topics: Interests versus positions; BATNA and ZOPA; Mutual gains and objective criteria; Dual-concern model; Anchoring, framing and concessions; Trade-offs and logrolling; Cognitive biases and influence; Power and emotions; Trust, reputation and ethics; Cross-cultural and organizational negotiation; Negotiation implementation and withdrawal; Stakeholder interests
courseEvidence.methods: BATNA and ZOPA analysis; Stakeholder-interest mapping; Interest-based negotiation; Negotiation simulations; Narrative and film analysis of bargaining; Negotiation-scene scripting and annotation; Scenario design and reflective evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: develops negotiation, strategic interaction and the psychology of influence

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Data Science
courseEvidence.description2: Develops foundational skills in data visualization, cleaning and manipulation. Explores spatial and text data and includes hands‑on work with datasets from various disciplines.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces data analysis and visualization in R through practical work with tabular, textual and spatial data. Students import, clean, transform and join data, explore patterns, and construct visualizations using tidy-data principles and the grammar of graphics. Web scraping and basic programming functions extend the workflow. A student research project applies these tools to a question using data from a field of interest.
courseEvidence.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions
courseEvidence.methods: R programming; ggplot visualization and grammar of graphics; Data cleaning, tidying and transformation; Data import and joins; Web scraping; Text-data analysis; Geospatial-data analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides foundational data cleaning, visualisation and analysis skills

courseEvidence.name: Machine Learning
courseEvidence.description2: Covers core machine learning techniques from linear regression to advanced tree‑based methods. Discusses strengths and weaknesses and applies methods to real data from fields like medicine, physics and economics.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces statistical learning for understanding data and predicting outcomes. Students study regression and classification, model accuracy, resampling, regularization, nonlinear models, trees, support vector machines and unsupervised learning. Practical assignments evaluate methods on real data using R or Python. Projects emphasize informative predictor construction, test-set prediction, appropriate model choice and clear reporting of results and limitations.
courseEvidence.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering
courseEvidence.methods: Linear and logistic regression; Generative classification; Cross-validation and bootstrap; Subset selection; Ridge regression and LASSO; Splines and generalized additive models; Basic and advanced decision-tree methods; Support vector machines; Principal component analysis; Clustering; Predictive-performance evaluation; R or Python implementation
courseEvidence.contribution: adds machine-learning methods for analysing complex behavioural and biological data

courseEvidence.name: Image Processing & Computer Vision
courseEvidence.description2: Covers processing and analysis of image data, including feature detection and tracking. Discusses applications in medicine, self‑driving vehicles, gaming, robotics and traffic management.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines how digital images are represented, processed and interpreted to recognize structures and objects. Spatial and spectral representations, colour and image statistics support filtering, segmentation, curve and feature detection, tracking and object classification. Students use Python and OpenCV to implement image-processing techniques, investigate spectral representations, and build a recognition pipeline whose performance is benchmarked on previously unseen images.
courseEvidence.topics: Spatial and spectral image representations; Cameras and calibration; Colour models and quantization; Image histograms; Point operators; Linear and nonlinear filters; Edges and contours; Mathematical morphology; Image segmentation; Curve and corner detection; Feature detection and tracking; Object localization and classification; Recognition performance
courseEvidence.methods: Python and OpenCV programming; Image filtering; Histogram and point transformations; Morphological image processing; Hough transform; Image segmentation; Feature matching and tracking; Recognition-pipeline design; Benchmark evaluation on unseen images
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses computational image representation and object recognition; these methods complement the study of human vision without substituting for it.

courseEvidence.name: Ethics
courseEvidence.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
courseEvidence.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
courseEvidence.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development
courseEvidence.contribution: provides ethical reasoning for evaluating policy, professional practice and institutional choices

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Sociology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
courseEvidence.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
courseEvidence.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation
courseEvidence.contribution: provides the foundational sociological concepts needed to analyse social structures and institutions

courseEvidence.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
courseEvidence.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
courseEvidence.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation
courseEvidence.contribution: provides qualitative research design, data collection and interpretation skills

courseEvidence.name: Modern Sociology
courseEvidence.description2: Examines the trajectory of sociology within the culture of imperialism and colonial responses. Studies leading social theories and debates about modernity and critically engages with sociological discourses.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines twentieth-century and contemporary social theory alongside critical accounts of modernity, colonialism and disciplinary exclusion. Functionalism, critical theory, Black feminist thought, phenomenology, symbolic interactionism and Bourdieu's work are read with postcolonial, decolonial and Indigenous perspectives. Students compare theories and apply them to empirical cases, including visual material. An individual research paper develops a theoretically grounded interpretation of a selected social phenomenon.
courseEvidence.topics: Modernity and Eurocentrism; Functionalism; Frankfurt School critical theory; Black feminist thought and intersectionality; Social construction of reality; Symbolic interactionism; Stigma and othering; Social space, capital and art; Coloniality and postcolonialism; Decolonial and Indigenous sociology; Gender and power
courseEvidence.methods: Close reading of social theory; Comparative theoretical analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Visual sociological analysis; Literature-based sociological research
courseEvidence.contribution: develops modern sociological theory needed before advanced contemporary social-theory work

courseEvidence.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
courseEvidence.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
courseEvidence.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.
courseEvidence.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative social-theory analysis; Theory-guided empirical case analysis; Document and secondary-source analysis; Structured reflection on civil-society engagement or observation; Sociological research design
courseEvidence.contribution: adds advanced analysis of contemporary social theory, civil society and institutional change

courseEvidence.name: Epidemiology & Public Health
courseEvidence.description2:
Public health is about changing the world. From pandemics to lifestyle-related diseases, from screening for disease to improving water and air quality, it asks: how can we improve to keep the population healthy?_x000D_
But how do we know what actually works? In this course you will dive into epidemiology: the science behind public health. You will learn how to study disease, risks, and changes over time, and how to critically evaluate evidence. Because behind every public health decision lies a question of evidence, and by the end of this course, you will be equipped to engage with it. This course invites you to look beyond the lab, the hospital, and the library, into the wider world where health is shaped. What matters most if we truly care about health, and how can we influence that?
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces epidemiological reasoning and its application to public health. Students measure and interpret disease patterns, study research designs, association, bias, confounding and causality, then examine health determinants, promotion, needs assessment and screening. A local project analyzes a Zeeland health challenge, compares population data, considers affected groups and interventions, and incorporates stakeholder perspectives into feasible recommendations.
courseEvidence.topics: Disease frequency and risk; Incidence and prevalence; Measures of association; Epidemiological study designs; Bias, confounding and causality; Outbreak investigation; Social and environmental health determinants; Health inequalities; Health promotion; Health-needs assessment; Screening; Evidence-informed interventions and implementation
courseEvidence.methods: Epidemiological rate and risk calculation; Descriptive and analytic epidemiology; Study-design and evidence appraisal; Population-health data interpretation; Outbreak analysis; Health-needs assessment; Stakeholder interviewing; Evidence-informed intervention development
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses population data to investigate health patterns and evaluate epidemiological evidence.

courseEvidence.name: Functional Anatomy
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces human body functioning using imaging, surface anatomy and dissection materials. Shows how anatomy serves function and discusses ethical considerations of learning from the dead.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies human anatomical structure in relation to function through regional and body-system blocks. Skeletal, thoracic, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, reproductive and lower urinary anatomy are developed through spatial reasoning, medical images, anatomical drawing and human-specimen material. Guided practicals and dissection-room observation connect three-dimensional relationships to variation. Historical, ethical and societal questions about human remains, representation and sex accompany the anatomical study; activities are framed as academic learning rather than clinical qualification.
courseEvidence.topics: Anatomical terminology and body planes; Medical imaging; Skeletal system and vertebral column; Thorax and pelvis; Respiratory and cardiovascular systems; Abdominal organs and vascular supply; Reproductive and lower urinary systems; Anatomical variation and intersex presentations; Human remains and dissection ethics; History and representation of the body
courseEvidence.methods: Surface-anatomy observation; Anatomical image interpretation; Scientific anatomical drawing; Three-dimensional anatomical reasoning; Guided study of human skeletal remains and anatomical specimens; Ethical reflection on anatomical practice
courseEvidence.contribution: provides functional anatomy linking bodily structure to physiological function

courseEvidence.name: Neurobiology
courseEvidence.description2: Examines evolution and complexity of brains. Explores animal cognition, welfare and research ethics and studies how brain regions and rhythms regulate behaviour through interactive assignments.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies nervous systems and behaviour from comparative, evolutionary and physiological perspectives. Brain anatomy and laboratory introductions support analysis of animal behaviour, research models and welfare. The second part connects regulatory behaviour and biological rhythms to sleep, lifestyle drugs, mood and eating disorders. Comparative-anatomy work and a literature-based disorder report apply neurobiological concepts while animal-research assignments examine reduction, refinement and replacement.
courseEvidence.topics: Nervous-system evolution and comparative anatomy; Brain cells and morphology; Cerebral circulation and nerves; Animal behaviour and welfare; Sentience and research ethics; Reduction, refinement and replacement; Enrichment and brain development; Regulatory and sexual behaviour; Lifestyle drugs; Circadian rhythms and sleep; Sleeping and eating disorders; Depression and anxiety; Gut-brain axis; Hypothalamus and pineal gland; Dying brain and consciousness
courseEvidence.methods: Comparative brain-anatomy analysis; Introductory microscopy and cell staining; Brain-model comparison; Ethical appraisal of animal research and the 3Rs; Literature-based analysis of neurobiological disorders
courseEvidence.contribution: provides neurobiological foundations for understanding cognition and brain-behaviour relations

courseEvidence.name: Perception & Action
courseEvidence.description2: Explores neural mechanisms behind perception and action. Examines how the brain processes sensory information and guides goal‑directed behaviour using methods from cognitive neuroscience and neuropsychology.
courseEvidence.contribution: examines neural mechanisms of perception and action

courseEvidence.name: Higher Order Functions
courseEvidence.description2: Deepens understanding of neurophysiology and neuroanatomy. Explores higher‑level cognitive functions—memory, emotion, social cognition, executive functioning and language—and engages with current research while designing experiments.
courseEvidence.profile: Deepens understanding of neuroanatomy, neurophysiology and the experimental study of higher cognitive functions. Students examine attention, memory, emotion, cognitive control, social cognition, pain and consciousness, connecting brain function and dysfunction to behaviour. An attentional-blink experiment provides direct engagement with empirical work. A team research proposal requires literature analysis, a feasible experimental design and ethical reflection, supported by peer review.
courseEvidence.topics: Neurotransmission and psychoactive drugs; Brain structure and hemispheric specialization; Attention and attentional blink; Memory and long-term potentiation; Emotion; Cognitive control and executive functions; Social cognition; Pain; Consciousness; Brain-behaviour relationships; Neuroscience research ethics
courseEvidence.methods: Cognitive-neuroscience experimental design; Attentional-blink experiment; Critical analysis of scientific literature and empirical data; Research-proposal development; Scientific peer review
courseEvidence.contribution: develops advanced understanding of memory, attention, executive functions and higher cognition

courseEvidence.name: Psycholinguistics
courseEvidence.description2: Psycholinguistics is the study of the neurobiological and psychological factors that enable us to acquire, use, and understand language. Modern research draws on cognitive psychology, neuroscience, and computer science to investigate how language is processed. The course focuses primarily, though not exclusively, on the neuroscience of language. Students examine theoretical and experimental issues in speech production and comprehension, language impairments, the relationship between thought and language, and the evolution and acquisition of language. They also gain hands-on experience with experimental approaches to the study of language and develop an understanding of human linguistic capacity as a subject of multidisciplinary research. Topics covered: What is language? Evolutionary aspects of language and animal communication; language and thought; aphasia; language acquisition; bilingualism; speech comprehension; semantics; reading and dyslexia; speech production.
courseEvidence.contribution: examines language processing through psychological and neurobiological perspectives

courseEvidence.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces biochemistry, macromolecules, cells, organ systems, DNA and cell function. Connects fundamentals to health and disease and serves as a starting point for medicine, biomedical science, life science or public health; no lab experience needed.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces the molecular and cellular foundations of life and biomedical science. Students study biological molecules, cells and membranes, communication, enzymes and energy metabolism, cell division, DNA and heredity, gene expression, genomes and biotechnology. Scientific experiments and papers are analyzed through short teaching contributions and a research-based mini-symposium. A responsive final component selects additional life- and biomedical-science topics with the class.
courseEvidence.topics: Biological molecules and chemistry of life; Cells, organelles and membranes; Cellular communication; Enzymes and energy metabolism; Cell cycle and division; DNA and heredity; Gene mutation and molecular medicine; Gene-expression regulation and epigenetics; Genomes; Recombinant DNA and biotechnology
courseEvidence.methods: Scientific-literature searching and synthesis; Analysis of published biological experiments
courseEvidence.contribution: provides foundational life-science knowledge needed for biological and health-oriented study

courseEvidence.name: Introduction to Brain & Behavior
courseEvidence.description2: Explores why people behave as they do and how brain injuries affect mental processes. Discusses nature and nurture, introduces brain anatomy and psychological theories, and provides a gateway to cognitive science and clinical psychology.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces psychological and neuroscientific explanations of behaviour and mental processes. Students study neural signalling, brain anatomy and development, learning, intelligence, personality, social influence, mental disorders and treatments. Several sessions introduce behavioural, imaging and electrophysiological approaches to neuroscience and their combined use. Interdisciplinary research-article and case analysis connects psychological processes to neural mechanisms and clinical questions.
courseEvidence.topics: Brain and behaviour; Neural signalling and action potentials; Functional neuroanatomy; Brain development and hemispheric specialization; Associative, non-associative and social learning; Intelligence; Personality and self-concepts; Social influence; Mental disorders and DSM-5-TR; Psychological treatment; Neuroimaging, electrophysiology and converging methods
courseEvidence.methods: Psychological and neuroscientific research appraisal; Interdisciplinary case-study analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides the foundational psychology and neuroscience gateway for advanced behavioural and cognitive courses

courseEvidence.name: Molecular Cell Biology
courseEvidence.description2: Provides foundation for practical applications in life science. Focuses on cellular biology of eukaryotes and prokaryotes, revisits concepts from introductory courses, examines current research and encourages evaluating reproducibility and modernising methods.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies the molecular mechanisms underlying cellular structure, physiology and regulation, primarily in eukaryotes. Bioenergetics, proteins and membranes connect to genome replication, repair and gene expression, followed by trafficking, signalling, division, tissues, stem cells and cancer. Students evaluate research methods and reproducibility and investigate a drug's molecular target, therapeutic action, metabolism and adverse effects through primary literature, a paper and a research poster.
courseEvidence.topics: Cellular components and bioenergetics; Proteins and membranes; Cytoskeleton; DNA replication and repair; Genomes; Regulation of gene expression; Membrane transport and trafficking; Cell-signalling pathways; Cell division and fate; Tissue organization; Stem cells; Cancer; Molecular mechanisms of drug action
courseEvidence.methods: Critical analysis of primary molecular-biology literature; Evaluation of research-method limitations and reproducibility; Thermodynamic free-energy calculations; Molecular mechanism analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: provides molecular and cellular foundations for biological explanations of behaviour and health

courseEvidence.name: Human Physiology
courseEvidence.description2: Studies normal functioning of the human body, covering structure‑function relationships, energy handling, homeostasis, signalling, organ systems and integration of their functions.
courseEvidence.profile: Studies normal function and regulation in the adult human body, linking molecular and cellular processes to integrated organ systems. Homeostasis, signalling and energy handling frame nervous, endocrine, muscular, respiratory, cardiovascular, renal, digestive and reproductive functions. Medical examples illustrate physiological principles. An individual literature-based paper examines a selected physiological or pathophysiological process and is developed through structured peer review and revision.
courseEvidence.topics: Cells, tissues and membrane dynamics; Homeostasis and control; Cellular signalling; Endocrine and nervous regulation; Muscles and movement; Breathing and gas exchange; Blood and cardiovascular function; Renal function; Fluid and electrolyte balance; Digestion and metabolism; Growth and exercise physiology; Reproduction and development
courseEvidence.methods: Physiological literature review; Medline/PubMed literature searching; Scientific peer review and evidence-based revision
courseEvidence.contribution: provides the normal human-physiology foundation needed before pathophysiology

courseEvidence.name: Life Science Laboratory
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces biochemical and molecular laboratory work. Covers themes like blood, proteins, bacteria, DNA and bioinformatics and provides a foundation for clinical and biomedical research.
courseEvidence.profile: Provides hands-on training in biochemical, microbiological and molecular laboratory methods. Blood analysis, microbial culture and hygiene lead into bacterial transformation, green fluorescent protein production and purification, DNA isolation and analysis, and introductory bioinformatics. Students follow and sometimes adapt protocols, interpret experimental results, maintain reproducible laboratory records and communicate findings in scientific reports and figures.
courseEvidence.topics: Blood cells and proteins; Blood groups and hemograms; Aseptic culture and bacterial identification; Disinfection and sterilization; Antibiotic susceptibility; Genetically modified bacteria; GFP production and purification; DNA and plasmid analysis; PCR and restriction digestion; Protein and DNA databases; Genotype and population-genetic interpretation; Experimental reproducibility
courseEvidence.methods: Pipetting and workflow planning; Microscopy and blood-smear examination; Blood cell counting and hemogram measurement; ELISA; Aseptic culture and purity streaking; Bacterial identification and inhibition-zone testing; Sterilization and disinfection testing; pGLO bacterial transformation; Protein extraction and chromatographic purification; SDS-PAGE; DNA and plasmid isolation; PCR; Restriction digestion and agarose-gel electrophoresis; DNA and protein database searching; Laboratory notebook and scientific-report preparation
courseEvidence.contribution: develops laboratory, experimental and data-analysis skills in life science

courseEvidence.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
courseEvidence.description2: Covers general and molecular pathology and genetics. Studies cell injury, death, inflammation, immunity, tissue repair, regeneration, fibrosis and neoplasia, examines genetic mutations and diseases, and discusses genetic testing and ethical considerations.
courseEvidence.profile: Connects cellular pathology with the genetic mechanisms of human disease. Students examine injury and death, inflammation and repair, neoplasia and lymphoid malignancies, then inheritance, genetic variation, epigenetics, molecular diagnosis and genetic treatment. Ethical, legal and safety questions accompany genetic technologies. A two-year research-grant proposal integrates literature, hypotheses, method selection, controls, feasibility and budgeting; an ethics debate examines stakeholder positions.
courseEvidence.topics: Cell injury, adaptation and death; Acute and chronic inflammation; Regeneration, repair and fibrosis; Neoplasia; Pulmonary pathology; Leukemia and lymphoma; Genes, genomes and inheritance; Genetic variation and chromosome abnormalities; Gene regulation and epigenetics; Genotype-phenotype relationships; Genetic testing and DNA technologies; Gene-based therapies and cell manipulation; Genetics ethics, law and biosafety
courseEvidence.methods: Biomedical literature review; Research-grant proposal design; Hypothesis formulation and experimental-control selection; Research feasibility, timeline and budget planning; Stakeholder-based ethical argument analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: develops advanced understanding of molecular pathology and genetics

courseEvidence.name: Social Psychology
courseEvidence.description2: Covers main theories, findings and principles of social psychology, emphasising its scientific approach to understanding how people’s feelings, thoughts and behaviour are influenced by the presence of others.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces the scientific study of how thoughts, feelings and behaviour are shaped by other people and social situations. Social cognition, the self, influence and persuasion lead into group processes, prejudice, aggression, prosocial behaviour, attraction and close relationships. Students critically examine empirical research, synthesize findings from journal articles, formulate theory-guided questions and design a feasible study. The final project proposes research rather than conducting an empirical investigation.
courseEvidence.topics: Social cognition and person perception; The self and self-motives; Social influence; Persuasion, attitudes and behaviour; Group processes; Prejudice, stereotyping and discrimination; Prejudice reduction; Interpersonal aggression; Prosocial behaviour; Interpersonal attraction and close relationships
courseEvidence.methods: Critical appraisal of empirical social-psychology research; Literature synthesis; Theory-guided hypothesis formulation; Research design for a proposed social-psychology study
courseEvidence.contribution: provides core social-psychology theory on attitudes, groups and interpersonal behaviour

courseEvidence.name: Statistics & Experimental Methods
courseEvidence.description2: The course is necessary for students who want to pursue master programs in psychology and adjacent disciplines, as well as research masters in the medical domain. It is highly recommended also for all those who want to be researchers in other domains. In addition to technical training, the course emphasizes clear academic communication. It will equip you with the skills necessary to apply advanced statistical techniques to real-world research problems. With a focus on practical application through case studies and data analysis projects, You will be able to choose the appropriate statistical model for various research scenarios and address common challenges in data interpretation.
courseEvidence.profile: Develops experimental-design knowledge and practical statistical analysis for health and behavioural research. Students choose, fit, diagnose and interpret multivariable models, comparing means, analyzing categorical outcomes and studying latent constructs. R, primarily through R Commander, supports repeated practical exercises; SPSS is an optional alternative. Data-analysis papers and a poster connect research questions and hypotheses to appropriate models, assumption checks, substantive interpretation and APA reporting.
courseEvidence.topics: Experimental, nonexperimental and quasi-experimental designs; Statistical inference; Correlation and regression; Model assumptions and diagnostics; Group comparisons; Covariate adjustment; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed designs; Categorical outcomes; Latent constructs and scale reliability; Effect size and power; Statistical reporting
courseEvidence.methods: R and R Commander data analysis; Multiple linear regression and dummy coding; Regression diagnostics; t-tests and nonparametric alternatives; ANOVA and ANCOVA; Factorial, repeated-measures and mixed-design ANOVA; Logistic regression; Exploratory factor analysis; Principal component analysis; Cronbach's alpha; APA statistical reporting
courseEvidence.contribution: provides advanced statistical and experimental methods for psychological research

courseEvidence.name: Psychopathology
courseEvidence.description2: The Psychopathology course offers a deep dive into the factors shaping mental health across the lifespan. Students will develop critical thinking skills, explore the bio-psycho-social approach, and gain a comprehensive understanding of mental health and its disorders. Through key concepts, research findings, and psychological assessment techniques, this course empowers individuals to promote wellness and make a meaningful impact in both personal and professional spheres.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines mental health and psychopathology across the lifespan using a biopsychosocial perspective. Historical views, classification and assessment frame biological, psychological, cultural and social explanations of disorders and treatment. Case-based work applies diagnostic concepts to varied presentations. A structured literature-based essay investigates a focused mental-health question through explicit searching, source selection, evidence appraisal and synthesis, with optional use of PRISMA reporting tools.
courseEvidence.topics: Mental-disorder concepts and stigma; Historical and contemporary psychopathology; Biopsychosocial causation; Clinical assessment and diagnostic classification; Stress and health; Anxiety and obsessive-compulsive disorders; Mood disorders; Somatic and dissociative disorders; Psychotic disorders; Eating and personality disorders; Substance-related and neurocognitive disorders; Sexuality and mental health; Childhood and adolescent disorders; Forensic psychology; Culture and emotion regulation
courseEvidence.methods: Diagnostic case analysis; Application and critique of DSM criteria; Biopsychosocial case formulation; Structured literature searching and screening; Source-quality appraisal; Evidence synthesis; Critical evaluation of etiological and intervention models
courseEvidence.contribution: examines mental disorders through psychological and biopsychosocial perspectives

courseEvidence.name: Medical & Health Psychology
courseEvidence.description2: Uses a biopsychosocial approach to explore how biological, psychological and socio‑cultural factors influence health and illness. Covers theories, research and interventions and focuses on the role of psychological expertise in medical settings.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines health and illness through interactions among biological, psychological and sociocultural factors. Health inequalities, behaviour and prevention lead into stress, symptoms, pain, medical consultation and treatment decisions. Chronic illness is considered from patients', families' and healthcare professionals' perspectives. Students analyze research, interventions and clinical cases, practice interviewing with attention to culture, and apply clinical-health formulation to understand support and quality of life in medical settings.
courseEvidence.topics: Biopsychosocial model; Health inequalities; Health-risk and protective behaviours; Behaviour-change models; Prevention; Stress and coping; Symptom perception; Somatic symptom disorders; Medical consultation; Shared decision-making; Doctor–patient communication; Pain; Chronic illness; Family and caregiver experiences; Quality of life; Cultural competence; Support for healthcare professionals
courseEvidence.methods: Psychological case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of health-psychology research and interventions; Clinical-health case formulation; Interviewing-skills practice; Cultural Formulation Interview analysis
courseEvidence.contribution: examines psychological determinants of health, illness and wellbeing using a biopsychosocial approach

courseEvidence.name: Psychodiagnostics & Psychotherapies
courseEvidence.description2: Introduces key theories, methods and practices in psychodiagnostics and psychotherapy. Covers psychological assessment techniques and psychotherapeutic approaches and builds practical competencies and clinical skills.
courseEvidence.profile: Introduces clinical psychological assessment and major psychotherapeutic approaches across the lifespan. Students study ethics, diagnostic systems, test reliability and validity, interviews, personality and cognitive assessment, then psychodynamic, behavioural, cognitive, humanistic, systemic and integrative treatments. Training sessions develop introductory administration, scoring and interpretation skills. A psychodiagnostic case report integrates findings and treatment recommendations, while self-monitoring examines developing clinical skills.
courseEvidence.topics: Clinical attitude and ethics; Diagnostic classification; Reliability and validity; Clinical interviews; Personality inventories and projective techniques; Cognitive and neuropsychological assessment; Behavioural and biological assessment; Psychological reporting; Psychodynamic and behavioural therapies; Cognitive therapy and CBT; Person-centered and family therapies; Integrative psychotherapy; Treatment outcomes and evidence; Child and adolescent clinical psychology
courseEvidence.methods: Clinical interviewing practice; Introductory psychological-test administration, scoring and interpretation; Psychometric appraisal; Behavioural observation; Integration of assessment data; Psychodiagnostic report writing; Clinical case and therapy-session analysis; Reflective monitoring of clinical skills
courseEvidence.contribution: develops knowledge of psychological assessment, psychodiagnostics and psychotherapeutic approaches

courseEvidence.name: Advanced Research Methods & Statistics
courseEvidence.description2: This course guides you through combining results from multiple studies using systematic reviews and meta-analysis a method now essential in psychology, medicine, social science and other disciplines. Want to know what really works? Gain hands-on skills in research synthesis that inform evidence-based policy and practice. You’ll search literature, manage data, and present findings that matter. Learn to calculate effect sizes, synthesize results and assess bias using R.
courseEvidence.profile: Teaches systematic review and meta-analysis for synthesizing evidence in medical, behavioural and related research. Students define review questions, search and select studies, extract and code findings, assess bias and compute effect sizes. Hands-on R work fits fixed- and random-effects models, examines heterogeneity and moderators, conducts meta-regression and investigates publication bias. A group project completes a small meta-analysis and presents its methods and results in a research poster.
courseEvidence.topics: Systematic-review purpose and limitations; Review protocols and scope; Literature searching and inclusion criteria; Data extraction and study coding; Risk of bias; Effect-size types and transformations; Fixed- and random-effects models; Effect heterogeneity; Moderators and subgroup differences; Meta-regression; Publication bias; Research synthesis and reporting
courseEvidence.methods: Systematic literature review; Database searching and study screening; Study-data extraction and coding; Critical risk-of-bias appraisal; R programming and data management; Effect-size calculation and conversion; Fixed- and random-effects meta-analysis; Moderator and subgroup analysis; Meta-regression; Publication-bias analysis; Meta-analytic visualization and reporting
courseEvidence.contribution: Uses systematic review, effect sizes and meta-analysis to synthesize evidence from multiple studies.

courseEvidence.name: Lifespan Developmental Psychology
courseEvidence.description2: Explores human development across the lifespan. Examines physical, cognitive, emotional and social changes from prenatal life to old age and develops critical thinking about factors influencing individual uniqueness.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines physical, cognitive, emotional, social and personality development from prenatal life through old age and death. Biological and environmental influences are considered alongside attachment, education, relationships, cultural differences and developmental psychopathology. Students connect theoretical perspectives to case studies, assessment and interventions at different life stages. A life-story interview with an adult over fifty applies developmental concepts through interviewing, analysis and a written report.
courseEvidence.topics: Developmental theories; Genetics and environment; Prenatal development and birth; Infancy and attachment; Cognitive and psychomotor development; Early and middle childhood; Play and education; Adolescence and psychopathology; Emerging and early adulthood; Middle and late adulthood; Relationships and personality development; Care and developmental interventions; Death, dying, grief and bereavement
courseEvidence.methods: Life-story interviewing; Theory-guided lifespan interview analysis; Developmental case-study analysis; Critical appraisal of developmental research and assessment reports
courseEvidence.contribution: provides systematic study of cognitive, emotional and social development across the lifespan

courseEvidence.name: Youth Resilience to Extremism
courseEvidence.description2: Interdisciplinary course combining psychology and other social sciences in which students will have an opportunity to participate in an actual international research project and develop evidence-based materials for youth leaders and educators aimed at strengthening young people’s resilience to radicalization by promoting democratic school culture, emotionally supportive learning environments, empathy, civic engagement, and mental well-being.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines youth radicalization and educational prevention through psychology, education, sociology, political science and peace education. Models of radicalization and adolescent risk and protective factors lead into inclusive school climates, belonging, social-emotional learning, dialogue, media literacy and civic agency. Students translate primary research into teacher-training materials and a youth toolkit for an international school project, then revise the resources using feedback from intended recipients.
courseEvidence.topics: Radicalization, violent extremism and terrorism; Developmental and psychosocial pathways; Risk and protective factors; School climate and belonging; Identity and peer influence; Social-emotional learning and well-being; Empathy and perspective-taking; Conflict resolution and intercultural dialogue; Mental-health literacy and referral; Digital literacy and misinformation; Youth leadership and democratic participation; Counter- and alternative narratives
courseEvidence.methods: Primary-research synthesis; Intervention-evidence appraisal; Case and classroom-scenario analysis; Inclusive educational-resource design; Alternative-narrative development; Recipient-feedback collection and iterative revision; Ethical appraisal of prevention tools
courseEvidence.contribution: examines youth resilience, psychological wellbeing and evidence-based intervention in social contexts

courseEvidence.name: Persuasive Communication
courseEvidence.description2: Explores ethical persuasion and climate communication. Students learn persuasive communication models and frameworks and collaborate with climate scientists at the Delta Climate Centre to produce sustainability messaging on water, food and energy.
courseEvidence.profile: Examines contemporary persuasion through communication studies, social psychology and ethical analysis, then applies it in community-engaged work. Students study coactive persuasion, framing, argumentation, cognitive shortcuts and verbal and nonverbal communication. Projects with the Delta Climate Centre and Vlissingen municipality develop communication encouraging sustainable and circular lifestyles. An individual research paper evaluates selected persuasion tools through literature review, field research diaries and reflective analysis of their use.
courseEvidence.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication
courseEvidence.methods: Persuasive-message design; Communication consulting and implementation; Literature review; Qualitative research diaries; Action research; Reflective case-study analysis; Gibbs reflective cycle
courseEvidence.contribution: develops evidence-based persuasive communication, including social-psychological mechanisms and public applications

comparability.assessment: The broad option covers development, clinical and social psychology, cognition and behavioral methods. The brain option adds biological mechanisms, laboratory work and computation. The organizational option adds applied leadership, consumer behavior and organizational research. The clinical and development/trauma interests are visible within the broad option; separate professional clinical or specialist trauma curricula would overstate the depth of the available sequence.

repair: Broad: exchange Perception & Action and Psycholinguistics terms, and replace Behavioral Economics with Econometrics. Brain: exchange computer vision and Psycholinguistics terms, move the introductory population-health course ahead of Youth Resilience, and substitute Research Methods & Statistics for Mechanisms of Disease. Organizations: use Marketing & Consumer Engagement in the fourth term, schedule Behavioral Economics in the fifth term in place of International Business & Governance, and use Econometrics in the sixth. Both specialisations have distinctive progression. Brain adds molecular science, physiology and computational methods; organizational study adds foundations, leadership, negotiation and consumer and market methods. The broad option includes clinical assessment, psychopathology and development. The available clinical and trauma-related courses do not justify a separate professional or trauma-specialist sequence. The schedules do not include Leiden’s mandatory capstone or a distinct psychometrics course.
alignments: Both examine attitudes, groups and social influence. Leiden also introduces organizational psychology in this unit.
Both examine development. UCR follows development across the lifespan, while Leiden also addresses educational psychology.
Leiden requires a separate history of psychology course.
This plan reserves 10 EC for Psychology electives.
Leiden requires an introductory survey of psychology. UCR’s gateway combines psychological and neuroscience foundations.
Both introduce neural and psychological explanations of behavior. UCR combines this with broader psychological foundations.
Both introduce clinical and mental-health questions. UCR focuses on psychopathology and the biopsychosocial context of mental health.
Both introduce psychological assessment. UCR also surveys psychotherapy approaches.
Both study neural mechanisms of cognition. UCR focuses on perception and action, while Leiden’s specialisation covers a wider range of topics and methods.
Both study attention, memory and other cognitive processes. UCR emphasizes their neural and experimental foundations.
Leiden requires a course on stress, health and illness. UCR addresses related topics within medical and health psychology.
Leiden requires a separate developmental psychopathology course. UCR studies development and psychopathology in broader courses.
Leiden requires a separate consciousness course.
Both examine motivation, group processes and organizational culture. UCR applies these ideas to leadership and organizational behavior.
Leiden requires a separate unit in interpersonal professional skills for psychology.
Leiden requires a separate Group Dynamics course. UCR addresses group processes in social psychology and leadership.
Both teach statistical inference in psychological research. UCR combines statistics with experimental design.
Both develop critical evaluation of research. UCR focuses on systematic reviews and meta-analysis.
Both develop empirical research design and statistical analysis. UCR includes a group research project.
Leiden requires a separate course in psychological measurement and test quality.
Leiden requires a psychology course in multivariate methods. UCR offers econometric modeling in two options.
Leiden requires a 15 EC psychology research project. UCR’s optional independent research is outside the scheduled 180 EC.
Leiden’s tutorial develops academic skills for psychology. UCR develops general academic skills in Personal & Professional Development.
Leiden requires an experimental and correlational research course. UCR teaches experimental design and applied statistics within its methods sequence.
Leiden requires a psychology-specific career planning unit.
This plan reserves 30 EC for open study.

candidates.label: A brain and cognition route centred on cognitive neuroscience, perception, learning, memory and language.
A social and organisational psychology route centred on social influence, groups, organisations, leadership and applied behavioural research.
A clinical-psychology and mental-health direction centred on psychological problems, clinical psychology and health.
candidates.reason: The broad option already includes psychopathology, assessment, health psychology and development. A separate clinical option would either repeat those courses or imply a more extensive clinical training sequence.

candidates.label: A development, trauma and child-abuse direction spanning the lifespan.
candidates.reason: Developmental psychology, psychopathology and youth resilience support parts of the direction. The broad option covers these interests, while specialist child abuse and neglect coursework remains a gap.
